source.title: AdaFlood: Adaptive Flood Regularization
source.authors: Wonho Bae; Yi Ren; Mohamed Osama Ahmed; Frederick Tung; D. Sutherland; Gabriel L. Oliveira

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a different explicit regularizer, flooding, changes held-out performance; it does not test the specific methods or measurements in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: Reports held-out metrics comparing flooding methods with unregularized models and with or without L2 regularization. The study does not report training error alongside test error, so these results do not measure the training–test gap. Hyperparameter search values and cited prior results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates adaptive flooding, not any of V1–V8. It cites memorization capacity and dropout as background. Its image experiments compare flooding and L2 regularization; they do not vary dropout, architecture, width, optimizer or batch size, measure magnitude-aware sharpness, or remove memorized examples. Appendix A demonstrates fitting some incorrect labels but does not test V1's paired natural-label and fixed-random-label generalization comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that instance-specific flood levels make AdaFlood broadly applicable across tasks and domains, improve robustness to label noise and calibration, and can be computed more efficiently through auxiliary-model fine-tuning. They explicitly qualify the image results by reporting no significant benefit on SVHN.
record.recipe_differences: Uses adaptive flooding, which selects an instance-specific target from auxiliary-model predictions; the listed versions concern other regularizers, architectures, optimizers, batch sizes, measures, or example removal.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by dataset and by whether L2 regularization is used; AdaFlood's advantage is reported on harder image datasets, while flooding methods are not significantly better on SVHN.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 2 compares flooding methods with and without L2. AdaFlood raises CIFAR10 accuracy from 87.80 to 88.38 without L2 and from 90.35 to 90.82 with L2; corresponding CIFAR100 changes are 56.59 to 57.25 and 61.49 to 62.31. The authors report no significant improvement on SVHN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Instance-adaptive flooding can improve image-classification accuracy over training without flooding on harder datasets, with benefits depending on the dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix A, Figure 6 shows a two-layer ReLU MLP reaching low training loss on regular, irregular and mislabeled synthetic Gaussian examples. Mislabeled examples retain higher loss when evaluated using a model trained on an independent dataset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-set losses can conceal incorrect labels that independent-data evaluation reveals; this motivates held-out estimates of sample difficulty.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code will be released in the final version.
record.problems: Image results are reported as test accuracy without corresponding training error, so they do not quantify the train–test gap. Image results use three runs and standard errors; authors report no significant improvement on SVHN.
record.rows_left_out: Section 4.1 Table 1 reports test metrics for flooding methods on event-sequence datasets; omitted because those density-estimation metrics are outside the claim versions' image-classification and train–test-gap outcomes. Sections 4.3–4.5 and figures report noisy-label, calibration, and auxiliary-training results; these address noise robustness, calibration, or implementation efficiency rather than the listed versions.

untested.parts: The same architecture and recipe fitting fixed random labels while generalizing on natural labels, with random-label held-out performance at chance.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, local connectivity, and convolution-derived initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, and optimizer switching.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce large-batch penalties.
Dropout interventions, small-data and excessive-dropout regimes, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and its ranking of generalization gaps against other measures.
Removing examples selected by memorization influence versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All Table 2 values and standard errors in the record match the supplied text. These are method-performance comparisons outside V1–V8, so their directional states cannot serve as claim verdicts. Missing training–test gaps are specifically relevant to V7; their absence is not the general reason these experiments fail to test the other versions. Appendix A is not declared in rows_left_out, but its result fits no listed version and therefore does not require a missing claim-result entry.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization using the same architecture and recipe.
Width sweep past the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures or local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and tuning effects.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations to large-batch training.
Dropout's effect on held-out error, including small-data and over-regularization conditions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness or other measured properties tracking the training–test gap.
Removal of memorized examples and its effect on test accuracy.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates flooding regularizers without testing or operationally using V1–V8. Appendix A demonstrates memorization of some incorrect labels, but does not supply V1's natural-label versus random-label training and held-out comparison.

source_check.notes: All sampled rows are method-performance comparisons outside V1–V8; their values are correct, but they should not serve as evidence for these versions. The paper's Unreg. label means without flooding in the L2 columns, including R13 and R17; the authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate.
